chunks: Al-Bazawfari from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Malik from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn 'Atiyyah who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a mukatab (a slave who has contracted to pay a sum for his freedom) who died without paying off his contract, leaving wealth and a son. Who inherits him? He said: "If his master, at the time of contracting, stipulated that if he were unable to pay the installments, he would return to slavery, and he had indeed become unable to pay the installments, then whatever wealth he left belongs to the master, and his son returns to slavery. If his son was free after him, or if the master had contracted with him and his son together, [the ruling differs]. And if he did not stipulate that for him, then his son is free and pays on behalf of his father whatever remained of what his father left. The son has no share [of the estate] until he pays what is due upon him. And if his father left nothing, then there is nothing upon the son."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His saying (peace be upon him) 'and if his father left nothing, then there is nothing upon the son' is to be understood as meaning that the son is not liable for more than what remained due on his father, because we have clarified in the preceding narration, which Jamil narrated from Mihran, that if he had no wealth, his son would strive to pay what remained due on the father, and then he would become free after that.

key_terms.رَدٌّ فِي الرَّقِّ: Returning to slavery; the status of being re-enslaved.
key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has contracted with his master to pay a specific sum in installments in exchange for his freedom.
key_terms.نُجُومِهِ: The installments or scheduled payments of the mukatab's contract.

ai.seo_question: What happens to the son and estate of a mukatab who dies with unpaid installments?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the fiqh of *kitabah* (manumission contract), specifically addressing the inheritance of the estate and the status of the son when a mukatab dies with unpaid installments. It highlights the juristic distinction between a master's explicit stipulation of re-enslavement upon default versus the default rule where the son inherits the debt obligation but retains freedom, a nuance clarified by Shaykh al-Tusi to ensure the son is not burdened beyond the father's remaining debt. This reflects the Shia emphasis on contractual precision and the equitable distribution of financial liability within the family unit.
